chapter.name: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

questions.q: Differentiate, with one example each from the chapter, between a reason it gives for food varying from one region of India to another and a reason it gives for cooking practices changing over time.
questions.a: Region to region: the locally grown crops (with taste preferences, culture and traditions), for example ragi grown in Karnataka and ragi mudde eaten there. Over time: technological development, improved transportation or better communication, for example the electrical grinder replacing the sil-batta.
s: a reason for regional variety (local crops, taste, culture or tradition) with an example
a reason for change over time (technology, transport or communication) with an example of a changed tool

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Everything in Table 3.2 is made from the crops in its own state's crop column, and nothing else decides what people eat.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The traditional food is usually based on crops grown in the state, but the chapter also names taste preferences, culture and traditions.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: food is usually based on locally grown crops
What is missing: taste preferences, culture and traditions also matter

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with what the chapter would call it (column II).
Column I: 1. A family learns a new recipe from a cooking video on a phone  2. Trucks start bringing gas cylinders up to a hill village  3. A new grinder grinds idli batter in five minutes instead of an hour on a sil-batta  4. A family in Punjab makes makki di roti from maize grown on its own field
Column II: a. improved transportation  b. food based on a locally grown crop  c. better communication  d. technological development
Write a short household situation (two or three lines) in which an electrical grinder replaces a sil-batta, and name which factor from the chapter your situation shows.
questions.a: A family stops grinding chutney manually on a sil-batta and buys an electrical grinder because it makes grinding easier; the factor is technological development.
s: situation correctly pairs sil-batta (manual, earlier) with the electrical grinder (modern)
the benefit shown is ease of grinding
names the factor, technological development

questions.q:
Kamala in Mysuru spends 45 minutes each day grinding batter and chutney on a sil-batta. An electrical grinder would take 10 minutes a day, costs Rs 3,200 and adds about Rs 15 a month in electricity. Her mother values Kamala's time at Rs 40 an hour. Take a month as 30 days.
(a) How many hours does the grinder save in a month?
(b) Does buying the grinder change what the family eats or how its food is prepared? Give the chapter's term for this.
(c) Find the net monthly saving in rupees and the number of whole months after which the grinder has paid for itself.
(d) Her mother will buy the grinder only if it pays for itself within 6 months, and her grandmother wants to keep making coconut chutney the way she likes it on the sil-batta. What should the family do? Use (c).
questions.a: (a) 17.5 h (b) How the food is prepared: it is a change in culinary (cooking) practice; the batter and chutney stay the same. (c) 17.5 x 40 - 15 = Rs 685 a month; 3200/685 = 4.67, so 5 whole months (d) Buy the grinder, since 5 months is within 6, and keep the sil-batta for the grandmother's chutney, a matter of taste preference.
s: a change in how food is prepared: a culinary practice
net Rs 685 a month, so 5 months
buy the grinder (5 is within 6 months) and keep the sil-batta for the chutney

questions.q: True or False? Because India is an agricultural country, the same main crops are grown in all its regions, so food differs between states only because of taste. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. India has diverse soil and climate types, so different crops are grown in different regions (Punjab grows maize and wheat, Manipur grows rice, bamboo and soya bean), and the traditional food of a state is usually based on its own crops, along with taste, culture and traditions.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: diverse soil and climate give different crops in different regions, and food follows those crops as well as taste, culture and tradition

questions.q:
Mrs Bhat, 72, tells her grandson four things: (1) 'We still eat ragi mudde every week.' (2) 'I ground chutney on a stone; your mother uses a mixer-grinder.' (3) 'Trucks now bring vegetables to our town from other states.' (4) 'We grow ragi on our own land.'
(a) Which of her statements describes a change in culinary practice?
(b) Which statement gives a cause of such change, and which of the chapter's factors is it?
questions.a: (a) Statement 2: the stone (sil-batta) replaced by an electrical grinder. (b) Statement 3: improved transportation.
s: (a) statement 2, the sil-batta giving way to the electrical grinder
(b) statement 3, improved transportation

questions.q:
Punjab grows maize, wheat, chickpea and pulses; its traditional items are makki di roti, sarson da saag, chhole bhature, parantha, halwa and kheer, with lassi, chhach (buttermilk), milk and tea. Karnataka grows rice, ragi, urad and coconut; its items are idli, dosa, sambhar, coconut chutney, ragi mudde, palya, rasam and rice, with buttermilk, coffee and tea.
(i) Name one Punjab dish whose name shows a Punjab crop, and the crop.
(ii) Name two Karnataka dishes whose names show two different Karnataka crops.
(iii) Name every beverage that appears in both lists.
(iv) Count the food items plus beverages for each state.
(v) Both states grow four crops but list different totals. What does this show about whether the number of crops alone decides a menu?
questions.a: (i) Makki di roti, from maize. (ii) Ragi mudde (ragi) and coconut chutney (coconut). (iii) Buttermilk (chhach) and tea. (iv) Punjab 6 + 4 = 10; Karnataka 8 + 3 = 11. (v) It does not: equal numbers of crops give different menus, so taste preferences, culture and traditions also shape what is eaten.
s: makki di roti linked to maize
ragi mudde to ragi and coconut chutney to coconut
buttermilk (chhach) and tea
totals 10 and 11
crop count alone does not decide; taste, culture and traditions also matter

questions.q: Gopal claims, 'A region's traditional food is decided only by the crops grown there.' Which observation from the chapter's examples most weakens his claim?
questions.a: Karnataka and Manipur both grow rice, yet their dishes differ
o: Karnataka and Manipur both grow rice, yet their dishes differ
Punjab grows maize, and makki di roti is eaten in Punjab
Karnataka grows coconut, and coconut chutney is eaten there
Manipur grows rice, and rice is among its traditional items

questions.q: Shobha's family eats ragi mudde and rasam, and she says, 'Only Karnataka eats these, because the chapter's Table 3.2 (which shows Punjab, Karnataka and Manipur) lists them only under Karnataka.' (a) What is she assuming about the table? (b) Why is her conclusion not safe?
questions.a: (a) That the table covers every state. (b) It lists only three examples, and the chapter asks students to add more states; some items may be eaten in more than one.
s: (a) assumes the three-state table is a complete list of India
(b) the table is only a few worked examples, with an 'any other' row left open for more states

questions.q:
Statement 1: A region's soil type and climate affect which crops grow there, and so affect its traditional food.
Statement 2: The food a region eats depends only on the crops grown there.
Statement 3: The change from the sil-batta to the electrical grinder is a change in culinary practice.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
In 1975 Lakshmi in Mandya ground her chutney on a sil-batta and cooked ragi mudde on a chulha, using ragi from the family field. In 2025 her granddaughter cooks ragi mudde from the same field's ragi on a gas stove and grinds chutney in an electrical grinder.
(i) Name the modern tool that replaced each of the two old ones.
(ii) What has stayed the same over fifty years, and which idea of the chapter explains it?
(iii) What has changed, and what does the chapter call such practices?
(iv) A visitor says, 'Fifty years of change means Mandya's food no longer depends on its crops.' Evaluate this using (ii) and (iii). (2 marks)
questions.a: (i) Gas stove for the chulha; electrical grinder for the sil-batta. (ii) The dish, ragi mudde from locally grown ragi: traditional food is usually based on the crops grown in the region. (iii) The tools used to cook and grind: culinary (cooking) practices. (iv) The visitor is wrong: the change is in the tools, that is in how food is prepared, while the dish is still made from the local crop.
s: gas stove for chulha and electrical grinder for sil-batta
ragi mudde from local ragi stays, because food follows locally grown crops
the cooking and grinding tools changed: culinary practices
verdict: the visitor is wrong
reason: tools (practices) changed but the crop-based dish did not

questions.q: Gas cylinders first reached Ramesh's hill village only after a new road let delivery trucks drive up, and his family then stopped cooking on a chulha. Of the chapter's three factors, the road is an example of improved ___.
questions.a: transportation

questions.q: Dev looks at Table 3.2, sees tea listed as a beverage for Punjab, Karnataka and Manipur, and concludes, 'Tea is a food that every state of India eats, so food diversity is a myth.' Which reply is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Three examples cannot settle it; some items are shared, many are not
o: Three examples cannot settle it; some items are shared, many are not
He is right, since one shared item shows that every state eats alike
He is wrong, but only because tea is not grown in any of the three states
He is right, since beverages decide a state's food more than its crops do

questions.q: Priya's grandmother in Imphal learnt to make dosa by watching a cooking programme on television, and she now grinds the batter in an electrical grinder. Which pair of the chapter's factors does her story show?
questions.a: Better communication and technological development
o: Better communication and technological development
Improved transportation and locally grown crops
Taste preferences and improved transportation
Technological development and the climate of Manipur

questions.q: A cool hilly district and a hot coastal district of India have different soils. Explain, as a chain of three linked steps from the chapter, why their traditional dishes are likely to differ.
questions.a: Their soil types and climatic conditions differ; so different crops are grown in the two districts; and the traditional food of a region is usually based on its locally grown crops, so the dishes differ.
s: soil and climate differ between the districts
so different crops are grown in each
traditional food follows locally grown crops, so the dishes differ

questions.q:
(a) Karnataka grows rice, ragi, urad and coconut; Manipur grows rice, bamboo and soya bean. Which crop is named in both lists?
(b) That crop appears in both states' food lists, yet their menus are not the same. Name one dish exclusive to each state to show this.
questions.a: (a) Rice. (b) For example idli or dosa (Karnataka) and eromba or singju (Manipur): the other crops and traditions differ.
s: (a) rice is the crop named in both lists
(b) one dish found only in each state's list, showing the menus still differ

questions.q: Anita lists four facts about her family's kitchen in Hubballi. Which one is a change in culinary practice rather than a food choice linked to local crops or taste?
questions.a: Grinding chutney in a grinder instead of on a sil-batta
o: Grinding chutney in a grinder instead of on a sil-batta
Eating ragi mudde because the family farm grows ragi
Drinking coffee every morning because the family likes it
Serving coconut chutney because coconuts grow nearby

questions.q:
At a school food festival, three stalls show traditional items. Stall A: makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi. Stall B: eromba, singju, kangsoi, black tea. Stall C: idli, ragi mudde, coconut chutney, buttermilk. The organiser can keep only two stalls, and she wants the two whose states share a locally grown crop, so that she can buy that crop in one bulk order.
(a) Name the state each stall represents.
(b) For Stall C, link two of its items to two different crops grown in its state.
(c) Which crop is grown in both Stall B's and Stall C's states?
(d) Which two stalls should she keep, and what does the festival lose by her choice?
questions.a: (a) A Punjab, B Manipur, C Karnataka. (b) Ragi mudde from ragi and coconut chutney from coconut. (c) Rice. (d) Keep B and C, which share rice; the festival loses Punjab's food based on maize and wheat, such as makki di roti.
s: A Punjab, B Manipur, C Karnataka
ragi mudde to ragi and coconut chutney to coconut
rice is grown in both Manipur and Karnataka
keep B and C; Punjab's maize- and wheat-based dishes are lost

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many families in Karnataka now grind idli batter in an electrical grinder instead of on a sil-batta.
Reason (R): Rice and urad are among the locally grown crops of Karnataka.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Statement 1: Glucose is a fat that gives instant energy.
Statement 2: Fat is a source of stored energy.
Statement 3: Carbohydrates are the foods that help in growth and repair of the body.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: Write a short snack situation (two or three lines) for which this statement is true: 'All the energy-giving foods in this snack are fat sources, and none is a carbohydrate source.' Use three foods from the chapter and say why the statement holds.
questions.a: For example: on a long bus ride Arun eats roasted groundnuts, almonds and sunflower seeds. All three are listed by the chapter as sources of fat, and none is a cereal, a carbohydrate-rich vegetable, a fruit or sugar.
s: a clear situation with three foods
all three foods are fat sources from the chapter
no carbohydrate source (cereal, potato, fruit or sugar) is included

questions.q: Arjun says the sugar in his tea gives him no energy, because sugar is not a cereal, a vegetable or a fruit. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Common sugar is a type of carbohydrate, an energy-giving food
o: Common sugar is a type of carbohydrate, an energy-giving food
Sugar is a fat, so it gives only stored energy for later
Sugar is a protein, so it builds the body but gives no energy
Sugar is roughage, which gives no nutrients to the body

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Carbohydrates and fats are called energy-giving foods.
Reason (R): The only sources of carbohydrates and fats are plant foods.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Medu skipped breakfast and felt tired and less energetic by eleven o'clock. Which group of foods, by the chapter's name, did his body lack that morning?
(b) Next day his mother packs an aloo paratha made of wheat flour and potato. Explain why it suits the problem in (a).
questions.a: (a) Energy-giving foods (carbohydrates and fats). (b) Wheat and potato are both carbohydrate sources, and carbohydrates are one of the primary sources of energy, so the paratha gives him energy for his activities.
s: (a) energy-giving foods
(b) wheat and potato are carbohydrate sources, a primary source of energy

questions.q: A teacher asks for one carbohydrate source from each of the chapter's three groups: a cereal, a vegetable and a fruit. Which set does exactly that?
questions.a: Bajra, sweet potato and pineapple
o: Bajra, sweet potato and pineapple
Rice, banana and ripe mango
Wheat, potato and walnut
Potato, sweet potato and banana

questions.q: Show, using two examples from the chapter, that the statement 'every source of fat comes from plants' cannot be right.
questions.a: Butter and curd are animal-derived fat sources shown in the chapter, while it says sources of fat can be from plants or animals.
s: first animal-derived fat example (butter)
second animal-derived fat example (curd)
conclusion: fat sources come from both plants and animals

questions.q: Kunal skipped breakfast and feels tired and less energetic by eleven in the morning. The school shop sells boiled potato, paneer, pistachios and curd. Which one best fits 'an energy-giving food from the carbohydrate group'?
questions.a: Boiled potato
o: Boiled potato
Paneer cubes
Roasted pistachios
A bowl of curd

questions.q:
The school canteen in Jaipur sells sweet potato at Rs 15, roasted groundnuts at Rs 10, a banana at Rs 6, walnuts at Rs 40 and a pineapple slice at Rs 18 per serving. Latika has Rs 30. For a hike she wants one serving each of two different carbohydrate items and one serving of a fat item.
(a) Which of the five items are fat sources?
(b) Which two different carbohydrate items are cheapest, and what do they cost together?
(c) Can she afford her plan? Show the cheapest possible total.
(d) She decides to drop one carbohydrate item so that she spends as little as possible while still carrying one carbohydrate and one fat source. What does she buy, what does she spend, and which two kinds of energy does her snack still give?
questions.a: (a) Groundnuts and walnuts. (b) Banana and sweet potato, Rs 21. (c) No: the cheapest plan is 6 + 15 + 10 = Rs 31, more than Rs 30. (d) Banana and groundnuts for Rs 16: instant energy from the carbohydrate and stored energy from the fat.
s: groundnuts and walnuts
banana and sweet potato for Rs 21
cheapest total Rs 31, so No
banana and groundnuts, Rs 16, giving instant (carbohydrate) and stored (fat) energy

questions.q: True or False? A food does not have to be a carbohydrate source to be an energy-giving food. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Fats such as ghee, oils and groundnuts are also energy-giving foods; the chapter groups carbohydrates and fats together as energy-giving, and fat is a source of stored energy.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: fats (ghee, oils, nuts) also give energy; fat is stored energy

questions.q:
A grandmother in Ludhiana makes 20 winter laddoos from 360 g of wheat flour (aata), 180 g of ghee, 40 g of almonds and 20 g of pumpkin seeds, with a little edible gum that is not counted here. Her daughter suggests a lighter version with 450 g of aata and only 90 g of ghee, keeping the same almonds and seeds. The grandmother wants the laddoos to give energy that keeps the family warm through the cold mornings.
(a) Sort the four counted ingredients into carbohydrate sources and fat sources.
(b) What percentage of the grandmother's 600 g mix is made of fat-source ingredients?
(c) What is that percentage in the daughter's version?
(d) Which version suits the grandmother's purpose? Use (b), (c) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Carbohydrate: aata. Fat: ghee, almonds, pumpkin seeds. (b) (180 + 40 + 20)/600 = 40%. (c) (90 + 40 + 20)/600 = 25%. (d) The grandmother's version: it has more fat (40% against 25%), fat is a source of stored energy, and the chapter says laddoos rich in ghee and nuts give energy to keep us warm.
s: aata as carbohydrate; ghee, almonds and seeds as fat
the grandmother's richer-in-fat version, because fat is stored energy and ghee-and-nut laddoos keep us warm

questions.q: A marathon runner drinks glucose water during the race, but a trekker in the cold hills carries ghee laddoos. Using what the chapter says about each, explain the difference in their choices.
questions.a: Glucose, a carbohydrate, gives instant energy during a race; the ghee-rich laddoo is a fat source, a store of energy that also keeps one warm.
s: glucose gives instant energy for the race
fat is a source of stored energy, and ghee-rich food gives energy to keep warm

questions.q: Rhea notices that soya bean appears in the chapter's picture of fat sources and again in its picture of protein sources. She decides the book has made a mistake. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: One food can be a source of more than one food component
o: One food can be a source of more than one food component
Soya bean is listed twice by mistake; it is only a protein
Soya bean gives fat only when raw and protein only when cooked
A food that gives protein must also be a carbohydrate source

questions.q:
After the school food festival, Medu writes three notes. Note 1: 'Only sweet foods give us energy.' Note 2: 'Carbohydrates and fats are called energy-giving because they build and repair the body.' Note 3: 'Fats give energy, but carbohydrates do not.'
(i)-(iii) For each note, say what is wrong and give the correct idea with an example from the chapter.
(iv) His sister says a groundnut chikki, made of groundnuts and sugar, gives energy from two different food components. Is she right? Explain. (2 marks)
questions.a: (i) Wrong: cereals such as wheat and rice and vegetables such as potato are carbohydrate sources though not sweet, and fats such as ghee also give energy. (ii) Wrong: they are energy-giving because they provide energy for our activities; growth and repair is the work of proteins, the body-building foods. (iii) Wrong: carbohydrates are one of the primary sources of energy; glucose, a carbohydrate, gives instant energy. (iv) Yes: groundnuts are a source of fat and common sugar is a carbohydrate, and both are energy-giving.
s: note 1 corrected: non-sweet cereals and potato, and fats, also give energy
note 2 corrected: energy for activities; growth and repair is protein
note 3 corrected: carbohydrates are a primary energy source (glucose)
groundnut is a fat source and sugar a carbohydrate
so yes, two energy-giving components

questions.q: Which tiffin has NO energy-giving food from the fat group?
questions.a: Rice, potato curry and a banana
o: Rice, potato curry and a banana
Rice with ghee and a banana
Potato with groundnut chutney
Bajra roti with sesame seeds

questions.q: A snack list reads: groundnut, banana, pineapple, butter, walnut, mango, potato. The number of items that the chapter lists as fat sources is ___.

Coconut appears in the chapter both as a source of fat and among Karnataka's locally grown crops. A Karnataka breakfast is idli, made mainly from rice, with coconut chutney.
(a) Which energy-giving component does the chutney add?
(b) Which energy-giving component does the idli supply, and what does that mean for the breakfast as a whole?
questions.a: (a) Fat (from coconut). (b) Carbohydrate (rice is a cereal); so the breakfast supplies both energy-giving components, carbohydrate and fat.
s: (a) fat from coconut
(b) carbohydrate from rice, so both energy-giving components are present

questions.q:
Kiran says, 'A plate of boiled sweet potato and a ripe mango are energy-giving foods from the same food component.'
(a) Is she right? Name the component.
(b) Into which of the chapter's groups of sources does each food fall?
questions.a: (a) Yes: both are carbohydrate sources, and carbohydrates are energy-giving. (b) Sweet potato is a vegetable source and mango a fruit source of carbohydrate.
s: (a) yes, both are carbohydrates
(b) sweet potato a vegetable, mango a fruit

questions.q: Rohit says, 'A bajra roti and a spoon of ghee both give energy, so they must belong to the same food component.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Both are energy-giving foods, but bajra is a cereal and so a carbohydrate source, while ghee is a fat. Giving energy is shared by two different components, so it does not make them one component.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
bajra is a carbohydrate (cereal) and ghee is a fat
carbohydrates and fats are both energy-giving, so energy alone does not decide the component

questions.q: Asha says, 'Butter and curd are fat sources that come from animals.' Bilal says, 'Sunflower seeds and pumpkin seeds are fat sources that come from plants.' Who is right?
questions.a: Both of them
o: Both of them
Only Asha, since seeds give carbohydrate
Only Bilal, since animal foods give only protein
Neither, since fat comes only from ghee and oils

questions.q:
Jaya is trekking for a week in the cold hills of Sikkim and has packed bananas, walnuts, ghee laddoos made with wheat flour, glucose powder and sweet potatoes.
(i) Sort the five items into mainly carbohydrate sources, fat sources, or both. (2 marks)
(ii) On a steep climb she suddenly feels tired. Which item gives her energy fastest, and why?
(iii) Which single item supplies both an energy-giving carbohydrate and fat by itself?
(iv) To save space she must leave behind either the bananas or the sweet potatoes. Does that change the kinds of energy her bag can supply? Justify.
questions.a: (i) Carbohydrate: bananas, glucose powder, sweet potatoes. Fat: walnuts. Both: the ghee laddoos (wheat flour with ghee). (ii) Glucose powder: glucose is a carbohydrate that gives instant energy. (iii) The ghee laddoos. (iv) No: whichever she keeps is still a carbohydrate source, and glucose is a carbohydrate too, while walnuts and ghee still give stored energy from fat.
s: bananas, glucose and sweet potatoes as carbohydrate; walnuts as fat
the laddoos as both (aata and ghee)
glucose, because it gives instant energy
the ghee laddoos
no change: a carbohydrate source and fat sources remain

questions.q: Imran, aged ten, sees well in bright daylight but stumbles in dim evening light. Which pair of foods from the chapter's chart would best help him?
questions.a: Carrot and papaya, sources of vitamin A
o: Carrot and papaya, sources of vitamin A
Lemon and guava, sources of vitamin C
Paneer and curd, sources of calcium
Beetroot and pomegranate, sources of iron

questions.q: Explain why lemons and oranges cured the sailors in Case 1 but would not be the chapter's remedy for the neck swelling in Case 2.
questions.a: Sailors' bleeding and swollen gums were scurvy, a vitamin C deficiency, and lemons and oranges give vitamin C. The neck swelling is goitre, an iodine deficiency, which needs an iodine source such as iodised salt.
s: scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency and citrus fruit supplies vitamin C
goitre is an iodine deficiency
so the remedy for goitre is an iodine source such as iodised salt

questions.q:
Match each person (column I) with the change that best helps, according to the chapter's chart (column II).
Column I: 1. A sailor on a long voyage with no fresh fruit has bleeding gums  2. A child who is kept indoors all day has soft and bent bones  3. Villagers whose soil is low in iodine have swelling at the front of the neck  4. A girl who never eats green leafy vegetables feels weak and short of breath
Column II: a. iodised salt  b. more exposure to sunlight  c. beetroot and pomegranate  d. amla and guava

Ravi says, 'Water gives no nutrients, so I do not need to drink it if I eat enough food.'
(a) Is water one of the nutrients named by the chapter?
(b) Give one reason from the chapter why Ravi is still wrong.
questions.a: (a) No: the major nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. (b) Water is still an essential part of the diet: it helps the body absorb nutrients from food and removes waste through sweat and urine.
s: (a) no, water is not among the nutrients
(b) it helps absorb nutrients or removes waste through sweat and urine, so it is essential

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Iodised salt visibly reduced the swelling at the front of the neck in the region described in the chapter.
Reason (R): Common salt can be obtained from seawater or from rocks.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Farhan says, 'Iodised salt is common salt mixed with salts of iodine. It reduced neck swelling in the Himalayan region because the soil there was short of iodine.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes. He states the meaning of iodised salt correctly. The swelling (goitre) was due to an iodine lack in the soil, and so in the local food and water.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
iodised salt is common salt mixed with required quantities of iodine salts
the soil lacked iodine, so local food and water lacked it, causing goitre

questions.q: Tara, aged 12, eats no milk products, and her doctor says she needs more body-building food for her growth. Which plate fits the advice best?
questions.a: Tuar dal, peas and kidney beans
o: Tuar dal, peas and kidney beans
Rice, potato and a ripe banana
Groundnuts fried in ghee with butter
Carrot, papaya and a sweet mango

questions.q:
A doctor sees three patients. P has weak bones and tooth decay. Q, who rarely goes outdoors, has soft and bent bones. R has swelling and a burning feeling in the feet and hands, and trouble breathing.
(i) Name P's disorder and the mineral lacking.
(ii) Name Q's disease and the vitamin lacking.
(iii) Name R's disease and the vitamin lacking.
(iv) Q lacks a vitamin, yet the trouble shows up in the bones. Explain using the chart.
(v) Name the one food in the chart's source lists that supplies both P's and Q's missing nutrients.
questions.a: (i) Bone and tooth decay; calcium. (ii) Rickets; vitamin D. (iii) Beriberi; vitamin B1. (iv) Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for bone and teeth health, so without it calcium is not taken in and the bones become soft and bent. (v) Milk (listed for both calcium and vitamin D).
s: P: bone and tooth decay, calcium
Q: rickets, vitamin D
R: beriberi, vitamin B1
vitamin D helps absorb calcium for bones
milk

questions.q: True or False? Since vitamins and minerals are needed only in small amounts, a diet without them for a long time would cause little harm. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. They are small in quantity but essential, and a lack of one or more nutrients for a long time leads to deficiency diseases and disorders.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: small amounts are still essential, and long-term lack causes deficiency diseases

questions.q: Write a short diet history (two or three lines) of a student whose symptoms point to iron deficiency, naming the symptoms and the foods missing.
questions.a: A student feels weak and short of breath, and her meals have no green leafy vegetables, beetroot or pomegranate; the disorder is anaemia.
s: symptoms weakness and shortness of breath
missing iron sources named from the chapter
names the disorder, anaemia

questions.q: A school decides to add a fresh fruit to every child's lunch. Which reason for this is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Fruits supply vitamins and dietary fibre that keep the body healthy
o: Fruits supply vitamins and dietary fibre that keep the body healthy
Fruits are the main body-building food that growing children need
Fruits contain water, so children need not drink water at school
Fruits are fat sources that store energy for the cold months

questions.q: Compare Case 1 (the sailors) and Case 2 (the Himalayan region) on these points. (i) Symptom. (ii) Disease. (iii) Nutrient lacking. (iv) Remedy used. (v) Does either case show that the cause of the symptoms was simply too little food? Justify.
questions.a: (i) bleeding and swollen gums; swelling at the front of the neck. (ii) scurvy; goitre. (iii) vitamin C; iodine. (iv) lemons and oranges; iodised salt. (v) No: both were a lack of one nutrient, not of food in general (iodine was missing from the soil, food and water).
s: symptoms of both cases
scurvy and goitre
vitamin C and iodine
lemons and oranges; iodised salt
a lack of a particular nutrient, not of food as such, with a reason

questions.q: True or False? A person who eats enough food every day can still develop a deficiency disease. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. A deficiency disease comes from a lack of one or more particular nutrients over a long time, not from too little food; in the chapter's Case 2 people ate their local food but it lacked iodine, and they developed goitre.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a long-term lack of a particular nutrient causes it, as with iodine-poor local food and goitre

questions.q: Mr Rao, aged 70, has difficulty passing stool, and his doctor advises food high in fibre. Which breakfast tray suits the advice?
questions.a: Leafy vegetables, fresh fruit and wholegrain roti
o: Leafy vegetables, fresh fruit and wholegrain roti
Glucose water, sugar-rich sweets and a carbonated drink
Butter on paneer, with a ghee laddoo and milk
A glass of plain milk with a cup of sweet tea

questions.q: Differentiate between body-building foods and protective nutrients: give the job of each and one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Body-building foods are protein-rich foods that help in growth and repair of the body, for example pulses or paneer. Protective nutrients are vitamins and minerals, which protect the body from diseases and keep it healthy, for example vitamin C (amla) or iron (beetroot).
s: body-building: proteins for growth and repair, with an example
protective: vitamins and minerals that protect from diseases, with an example

questions.q:
A school mess in Nagpur records illustrative values for one nutrient in a vegetable: 40 mg per 100 g when raw and 25 mg per 100 g after cooking at high heat. Each student is served 150 g. The cook says the cooked dish is softer, which the younger children like. A teacher proposes serving each 150 g as half raw salad and half cooked.
(a) The chapter names one nutrient that is lost in this way. Which nutrient is it, and what causes the loss?
(b) Find the percentage loss on cooking.
(c) Find the amount of the nutrient in one 150 g serving that is all raw, and in one that is all cooked.
(d) Does the teacher's half-and-half serving give more of the nutrient than the all-cooked serving, and by how much? State one washing precaution from the chapter for the raw half.
questions.a: (a) Vitamin C, lost because of the high heat of cooking. (b) (40 - 25)/40 = 37.5%. (c) 60 mg raw and 37.5 mg cooked. (d) Yes: 75 g raw gives 30 mg and 75 g cooked gives 18.75 mg, 48.75 mg in all, which is 11.25 mg more than 37.5 mg; the cooked half stays soft for the younger children. Wash the vegetables thoroughly, preferably before cutting or peeling, since washing cut or peeled pieces can lose some vitamins.
s: vitamin C, lost to high heat
60 mg raw and 37.5 mg cooked
48.75 mg, 11.25 mg more, with the washing precaution

questions.q: Which statement about cooking and vitamins is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Fruits need not be washed, because washing removes vitamins
o: Fruits need not be washed, because washing removes vitamins
High heat during cooking can destroy some vitamin C
Washing cut or peeled vegetables may result in loss of some vitamins
All fruits and vegetables should still be thoroughly washed before eating

questions.q:
A residential school in Dehradun checks its 120 students. 24 show weakness and shortness of breath, 9 show swelling at the front of the neck and 18 show bleeding gums with slow healing of wounds. The 9 students with neck swelling joined last month from a hill district whose soil is low in iodine; the school kitchen already uses iodised salt in every meal. This month the kitchen can add only one new kind of food, and it wants to help the largest number of students.
(a) Name the deficiency disease or disorder for each of the three groups.
(b) What percentage of the 120 students has weakness and shortness of breath?
(c) Name the nutrient lacking in that largest group and two foods from the chart that supply it.
(d) Which kind of food should the kitchen add this month? Use the numbers and the fact about salt.
questions.a: (a) Anaemia, goitre and scurvy. (b) 24/120 = 20%. (c) Iron: green leafy vegetables, beetroot or pomegranate. (d) Iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables and beetroot: anaemia is the largest group (24 against 18 with scurvy), and the goitre group is already getting iodised salt.
s: anaemia, goitre and scurvy
iron, with two chart sources
iron-rich food, because 24 is the largest group and iodised salt is already used

questions.q:
Statement 1: Animal foods are the only sources of protein.
Statement 2: Vitamins and minerals, needed in small amounts, are called protective nutrients.
Statement 3: Vitamin D can be made by the body on exposure to sunlight.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Ravi eats no milk, curd, cheese or paneer, and his dentist says he needs more calcium for his teeth. Which item from the chapter's chart can still supply it?
questions.a: A glass of soya milk
o: A glass of soya milk
A bowl of pomegranate
A plate of raw carrot
A slice of fresh guava

questions.q: A mess serves a raw guava salad on Monday and a guava dish boiled for a long time on Tuesday. (a) On which day will the students get more vitamin C from the guava? (b) Give the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Monday (raw). (b) Some vitamins like vitamin C are lost during cooking due to high heat.
s: (a) the raw salad
(b) high heat in cooking destroys some vitamin C

questions.q:
Pooja plays kabaddi, and her coach says sportspersons need more of one food component.
(a) Name the component and explain, using the chapter's name for foods rich in it, why she needs more of it.
(b) Give one plant source and one animal source of it that are not milk products.
questions.a: (a) Protein: protein-rich foods are body-building foods that help in growth and repair, and sportspersons need proteins in larger quantities to build their muscles. (b) Plant: pulses, beans, peas, soya bean or nuts; animal: egg, fish, meat or chicken.
s: (a) protein, a body-building food for growth, repair and muscles
(b) one plant and one non-milk animal source

questions.q: Aarti tests one crushed food. It turns violet after copper sulfate and then caustic soda are added, shows no blue-black colour with iodine, and leaves an oily patch on paper that lets light shine faintly through. Which nutrients has she detected?
questions.a: Protein and fat, but not starch
o: Protein and fat, but not starch
Starch and fat, but not protein
Starch and protein, but not fat
Only fat, as violet also means fat

questions.q: Four foods give these results. P: blue-black, an oily patch, violet. Q: no change with iodine, an oily patch, no violet. R: blue-black, no patch, no violet. S: no change, no patch, violet. Name the nutrients found in each, and say which foods show more than one nutrient.
questions.a: P: starch, fat, protein. Q: fat. R: starch. S: protein. P shows more than one nutrient.
s: P: all three; Q: fat only
R: starch only; S: protein only
only P shows more than one

questions.q: A group's record says: 'Butter, wrapped in paper: no patch seen, so butter has no fat.' Show that this record cannot be right, and say what the group should do.
questions.a: The chapter says that if oil or butter is present in a food item, it leaves an oily patch on the paper. So butter tested properly must leave an oily patch, and 'no patch' means the test was not done properly (for example the paper was not wrapped and pressed). The group should wrap the butter, press the paper and hold it against light: an oily patch through which light faintly shines shows fat.
s: butter leaves an oily patch on paper, by the chapter
so 'no patch, no fat' contradicts this; the test was done wrongly
repeat: wrap, press, hold to light and look for the oily patch

questions.q:
Statement 1: Diluted iodine solution turns violet when starch is present.
Statement 2: A food that contains a little water should be pressed on the paper and judged at once, without letting the paper dry.
Statement 3: The protein test uses two solutions, copper sulfate and caustic soda, added one after the other.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only
o: Statement 3 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: (a) Name the colour that shows a positive result in the starch test and in the protein test. (b) A student dips a protein-rich paste in iodine and sees no blue-black colour. Does this show the food has no protein? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Blue-black for starch, violet for protein. (b) No. Iodine tests for starch, not protein; protein needs the copper sulfate and caustic soda test.
s: (a) blue-black for starch and violet for protein
(b) no: the iodine test detects starch, not protein

questions.q:
A group's record sheet for four foods reads:
Food A: turned blue-black with iodine. Conclusion: protein present.
Food B: wrapped and pressed in paper; a patch appeared and the paper was held to the light at once, while still wet. Conclusion: fat present.
Food C: turned violet after copper sulfate and then caustic soda. Conclusion: protein present.
Food D: no blue-black with iodine, no patch on paper, violet in the protein test. Conclusion: starch and protein present.
The teacher will put up only conclusions that are correct.
(a) Which conclusion is already correct?
(b) Rewrite the conclusions for Foods A and D from their own observations.
(c) Why can Food B's conclusion not be corrected on paper alone?
(d) Which food must be tested again, and how should that test be done?
questions.a: (a) Food C. (b) A: starch present. D: protein present; starch and fat not detected. (c) The patch was read while the paper was wet, so it may be from water and not from oil; the observation itself is unreliable. (d) Food B: press it in paper, let the paper dry, then hold it against light; only an oily patch through which light faintly shines shows fat.
s: Food C
A: starch; D: protein only
B's wet patch may be water, so its observation cannot be trusted
re-test B: let the paper dry, then look for an oily patch against light

questions.q: True or False? A food that gives no blue-black colour with iodine solution may still contain a carbohydrate. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The iodine test detects starch, which is only one type of carbohydrate; sugar, for example, is a carbohydrate but does not turn blue-black with iodine.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: iodine shows only starch, one type of carbohydrate; sugar does not turn blue-black

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The protein test turns a food blue-black when protein is present.
Reason (R): A violet colour in the protein test indicates the presence of protein.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
A bottle in the lab has lost its label, and Mishti thinks it may be iodine solution. Her class has already found that a slice of potato turns blue-black with iodine.
(a) How can she use a potato slice to check her idea?
(b) What result would make her doubt that the bottle holds iodine solution?
questions.a: (a) Put 2-3 drops from the bottle on a potato slice and watch the colour; a blue-black colour supports her idea. (b) If the potato slice does not turn blue-black, the liquid is unlikely to be iodine solution.
s: (a) drops on the potato slice, looking for blue-black
(b) no blue-black on the potato would make her doubt it

questions.q: Karan says, 'My boiled gram turned violet in the protein test, so it cannot contain starch. I can skip the iodine test.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. The violet colour shows only that protein is present. A food may contain more than one nutrient, so the protein result says nothing about starch; only the iodine test (blue-black for starch) can tell him that.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
violet shows protein only; a food can contain several nutrients
starch can be judged only with the iodine test

questions.q: A class has three unlabelled samples: crushed peanuts, butter and boiled gram. Write a plan: (i) how to test one sample for starch; (ii) how to test it for fat; (iii) how to test it for protein; (iv) how to record the results; (v) why one sample might be positive in more than one test.
questions.a: (i) Place a small piece on a dish and add 2-3 drops of diluted iodine; blue-black means starch. (ii) Wrap in paper, press, let it dry if wet, hold against light; an oily patch means fat. (iii) Paste in a test tube with water, 2 drops copper sulfate, 10 drops caustic soda, shake and wait; violet means protein. (iv) Write the colours in a table such as Table 3.3. (v) A food may contain multiple nutrients, like peanuts with protein and fat.
s: starch test with diluted iodine and blue-black
fat test with paper and light
protein test with both solutions and violet
results recorded in a table of observations
foods can contain multiple nutrients

questions.q: For the chapter's protein test, a teacher prepares 6 test tubes of food paste and follows the stated number of drops of copper sulfate solution and of caustic soda solution for each tube. Counting both solutions, she uses ___ drops in all.
A food gives no blue-black colour with iodine, no oily patch on paper and no violet colour in the protein test. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: Starch, fat and protein were not detected; other nutrients need a lab
o: Starch, fat and protein were not detected; other nutrients need a lab
The food has no nutrients of any kind, so it has no value
The food must be plain water, since water fails every test
The tests were done wrongly, since every food passes one test

questions.q:
A school in Coimbatore has 30 mL of caustic soda solution and 5 mL of copper sulfate solution. A dropper gives about 20 drops per mL. Each protein-test tube needs 2 drops of copper sulfate and 10 drops of caustic soda. Class 6 has planned 40 tubes, but the chapter says this test may be demonstrated by the teacher, which would need only 8 tubes. At least 15 mL of caustic soda must be kept for Class 7's test next week.
(a) Which food component does this test detect, and what colour shows it?
(b) How many drops of caustic soda do 40 tubes need, and how many mL is that?
(c) How many mL of copper sulfate would 40 tubes use?
(d) Should Class 6 run 40 tubes or the 8-tube demonstration? Show the caustic soda left in each case.
questions.a: (a) Protein; violet. (b) 400 drops = 20 mL. (c) 80 drops = 4 mL. (d) The 8-tube demonstration: 40 tubes would leave only 30 - 20 = 10 mL of caustic soda, less than the 15 mL needed, while 8 tubes use 80 drops = 4 mL and leave 26 mL.
s: protein; violet
400 drops = 20 mL
80 drops = 4 mL
the demonstration: 10 mL left would be too little, 26 mL left is enough

questions.q: Kabir adds 2 drops of copper sulfate to a tube of paneer paste and to a tube of rice paste. He adds 10 drops of caustic soda to the paneer tube and it turns violet, but he forgets the caustic soda in the rice tube, which stays unchanged. Which conclusion is safe?
questions.a: Paneer has protein; the rice tube must be tested again
o: Paneer has protein; the rice tube must be tested again
Rice has no protein, since its tube did not turn violet
Paneer has fat, since violet is the sign of fat in food
Neither has protein, since one tube was left incomplete

questions.q:
Kavya wants to know whether a biscuit contains fat and protein.
(a) Which two tests should she run, and what result shows each nutrient?
(b) If both results are positive, what can she conclude, and which food in the chapter gave the same pair of results?
questions.a: (a) The paper test (an oily patch through which light faintly shines shows fat) and the copper sulfate and caustic soda test (violet shows protein). (b) The biscuit contains both fat and protein, so one food can have more than one nutrient; peanuts showed both proteins and fats.
s: (a) paper test for fat and copper sulfate with caustic soda for protein, with the signs
(b) both nutrients present, as with peanuts

questions.q: Write the three observations a student would record for a food that the class then concludes 'contains fat and protein but no starch'. Say which observation rules out starch.
questions.a: No blue-black colour with iodine (this rules out starch); an oily patch on the paper that lets light faintly shine through; a violet colour after copper sulfate and caustic soda.
s: no blue-black with iodine, which rules out starch
an oily patch on the paper
a violet colour with copper sulfate and caustic soda

questions.q: Powder X is mostly starch and powder Y is mostly protein, but their labels have fallen off. Using only one solution, which test tells them apart?
questions.a: Iodine drops: the one that turns blue-black is X
o: Iodine drops: the one that turns blue-black is X
Paper press: the one that leaves an oily patch is X
Copper sulfate only: the one that turns violet is Y
Iodine drops: the one that turns violet is Y

questions.q:
Match each observation (column I) with the inference (column II).
Column I: 1. blue-black after diluted iodine drops  2. an oily patch that lets light faintly shine through  3. violet after copper sulfate and caustic soda  4. no colour change after iodine drops on a cucumber slice
Column II: a. protein is present  b. starch is present  c. fat is present  d. starch was not detected in that food

Medu tests a piece of plain chapati: it turns blue-black with iodine and leaves no patch on paper.
(a) What does Medu now know about starch and fat in this chapati?
(b) His friend spreads butter on another piece and repeats the paper test. What change should they expect, and why?
questions.a: (a) Starch is present; fat was not detected. (b) An oily patch through which light faintly shines, because butter leaves an oily patch, which shows fat.
s: (a) starch present, fat not detected
(b) an oily patch appears, because butter contains fat

questions.q: A class tests five foods and records (tick = positive). Food A: starch, fat, protein. Food B: starch only. Food C: fat only. Food D: protein and fat. Food E: none of the three. (i) How many foods show more than one nutrient? (ii) How many show fat? (iii) What percentage of the foods show starch? (iv) Can the class say Food E has no nutrients at all? Why? (v) How many tubes turned violet?
questions.a: (i) 2 (ii) 3 (iii) 40% (iv) No: only starch, fat and protein were tested, and other nutrients need a laboratory. (v) 2
s: A and D: 2 foods
A, C and D: 3 foods
No: other nutrients were not tested and need a well-equipped laboratory
2 tubes (A and D)

questions.q: Sunil says, 'Wafers have 536 kcal against 355 kcal for chana, so wafers are the healthier snack because they give more energy.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. The extra energy comes with high fat (35.0 g against 6.26 g), and wafers are low in protein and fibre. Chana, with more protein and fibre, is the better choice.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
more energy comes with much more fat
chana has more protein and fibre, so it is the better choice

questions.q: Rahul has candy bars and carbonated drinks every day after school. Which risk does the chapter link to eating like this?
questions.a: He may become obese and suffer from health problems
o: He may become obese and suffer from health problems
He may get goitre, since candy bars lack iodised salt
He may run short of energy, since candy has no calories
He may get scurvy, since carbonated drinks lack iron

questions.q: True or False? Potato wafers are called junk food because they contain no nutrients at all. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The wafer label shows 53.0 g carbohydrate and 7.0 g protein per 100 g, so they do carry nutrients. They are junk food because they are high in calories from fat (35.0 g) and sugar while very low in proteins, minerals, vitamins and dietary fibre.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they have some carbohydrate and protein; junk means high sugar and fat calories with very little protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre

questions.q: A child's one-day menu is: breakfast, wheat parantha with curd; lunch, rice, tuar dal and a green leafy vegetable; snack, banana; dinner, roti and paneer. (i) Name two energy-giving items. (ii) Name two body-building items. (iii) Name one item that is a protective source. (iv) Name two roughage sources. (v) Which essential component is not listed, and what should the child do about it?
questions.a: (i) wheat parantha and rice (ii) tuar dal and paneer (iii) green leafy vegetable (iron) or curd (calcium) (iv) green leafy vegetable and banana (v) water: drink sufficient water regularly.
s: two carbohydrate items
tuar dal and paneer as protein
a correct protective source
two roughage sources from fruits, leafy vegetables or wholegrains
water is missing; drink enough regularly

questions.q: Ananya, aged 12, plays hockey every evening. Her grandfather, aged 70, mostly sits and reads. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Their needs differ in type and amount with age and activity
o: Their needs differ in type and amount with age and activity
Both need the same amounts, since they share one kitchen
Only the grandfather's needs differ, as only age counts
Only Ananya's needs differ, as only daily activity counts

questions.q:
Per 100 g, roasted chana has 58.58 g carbohydrate and potato wafers 53.0 g. Rina says, 'Chana has more carbohydrate, so chana must be the junk food.'
(a) What is wrong with her reasoning?
(b) Which label values does the chapter's description of junk food actually depend on? Use them to decide.
questions.a: (a) Carbohydrate content alone does not make a food junk; the chapter judges junk food by high calories from sugar and fat together with very low protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre. (b) Energy and fat (wafers 536 kcal, 35.0 g against chana 355 kcal, 6.26 g) and protein and fibre (wafers 7.0 g, 4.8 g against chana 18.64 g, 16.8 g): the wafers are the junk food.
s: (a) carbohydrate alone does not decide junk food
(b) high calories and fat with low protein and fibre point to the wafers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Roasted chana is a better regular snack than potato wafers.
Reason (R): Per 100 g, chana has more protein and dietary fibre and less fat than wafers.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: The label says potato wafers have 35.0 g of fat per 100 g. A 250 g family pack holds ___ g of fat.

Statement 1: The type and amount of nutrients needed vary with age and gender.
Statement 2: Junk foods are high in calories because of their sugar and fat content.
Statement 3: Roughage and water are not part of a balanced diet because they are not nutrients.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Neha says, 'A balanced diet means everyone in a family eats the same amount of the same foods, as long as all the nutrients are in it.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. A balanced diet does need all essential nutrients, with roughage and water. But it must give them in the right amount for each person, and the type and amount needed vary with age, gender, physical activity, health status and lifestyle, so family members need different amounts.
s: Verdict: partly right
right: all nutrients (with roughage and water) are needed
wrong: the right amount differs with age, gender, activity, health and lifestyle

questions.q:
A school canteen sells a Rs 10 pack of potato wafers (40 g) and a Rs 15 pack of roasted chana (60 g). Per 100 g, wafers give 536 kcal with 7.0 g protein and 4.8 g fibre; chana gives 355 kcal with 18.64 g protein and 16.8 g fibre. At present the canteen sells 90 wafer packs and 50 chana packs a day, earning Rs 2 profit on each wafer pack and Rs 3 on each chana pack. The principal's rule: stop selling any snack that fits the chapter's description of junk food, unless the canteen's daily profit would then fall below Rs 120.
(a) Find the energy in each pack.
(b) Find the protein and fibre in each pack.
(c) Which pack fits the chapter's description of junk food, and why?
(d) If students then buy only the same 50 chana packs, find the daily profit. Does the rule say the canteen should stop selling wafers?
questions.a: (a) Wafers 214.4 kcal, chana 213 kcal. (b) Wafers 2.8 g protein and 1.92 g fibre; chana 11.184 g protein and 10.08 g fibre. (c) The wafers: about the same energy but far less protein and fibre, with high fat. (d) Profit falls from Rs 330 to 50 x 3 = Rs 150, which is not below Rs 120, so yes, stop selling wafers.
s: 214.4 kcal and 213 kcal
protein and fibre of both packs
wafers are junk: similar energy, much less protein and fibre
profit Rs 150, not below Rs 120, so stop selling wafers

questions.q: Write two questions you would ask of a packaged snack's label to decide whether it is junk food.
questions.a: Is the energy high because of high sugar and fat? Are protein, dietary fibre, vitamins and minerals very low?
s: a question about high sugar and fat or high calories
a question about low protein, fibre, vitamins or minerals

questions.q: Raju's weekly diet, as he lists it, has rice, potatoes, ghee and sweets. Which gap should a balanced diet fill first?
questions.a: Body-building foods like pulses or milk, and protective fruits and vegetables
o: Body-building foods like pulses or milk, and protective fruits and vegetables
Nothing is missing, since carbohydrates and fats supply every component
Only roughage is missing, since rice and potato already give protein
Only water is missing, since the rest of the list is already balanced

questions.q:
Two snack labels give values per 100 g. Snack A (a cream biscuit): 480 kcal, fat 20 g, carbohydrate 70 g, protein 6 g, dietary fibre 2 g. Snack B (a roasted mixed snack): 380 kcal, fat 7 g, carbohydrate 62 g, protein 13 g, dietary fibre 11 g.
(i) Which snack fits the chapter's description of junk food? Quote two pairs of values as evidence. (2 marks)
(ii) A student says, 'Snack A has less fat than potato wafers (35.0 g), so it cannot be junk food.' Evaluate this.
(iii) Which snack is the better regular choice for a growing child, and why?
(iv) Why should even the better snack not become the child's whole diet?
questions.a: (i) Snack A: more energy (480 against 380 kcal) and fat (20 g against 7 g), with less protein (6 g against 13 g) and fibre (2 g against 11 g). (ii) Not safe: junk food is judged by high calories from sugar and fat together with very low protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre, and A still has high energy with very little protein and fibre. (iii) Snack B, which has more protein and fibre with less fat. (iv) A balanced diet needs all the essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amount, which no single snack supplies.
s: Snack A identified
two pairs of values as evidence (energy or fat higher, protein or fibre lower)
less fat than wafers does not clear it: high calories with low protein and fibre
Snack B, with its higher protein and fibre
a balanced diet needs all nutrients, roughage and water, not one food

questions.q:
Sonu eats biscuits, noodles and white bread but no vegetables or fruit, and he often has constipation.
(a) Which component of a balanced diet is his food short of?
(b) Suggest one change, and explain how it helps even though this component gives no nutrients.
questions.a: (a) Dietary fibre (roughage). (b) Add green leafy vegetables, fresh fruit, wholegrains or pulses; roughage helps the body get rid of undigested food and ensures smooth passage of stools.
s: (a) dietary fibre (roughage)
(b) a fibre-rich change, with how roughage helps the body get rid of undigested food

questions.q: A packet label gives values per 100 g. Potato wafers: 536 kcal, fat 35.0 g, carbohydrate 53.0 g, protein 7.0 g, dietary fibre 4.8 g. Roasted chana: 355 kcal, fat 6.26 g, carbohydrate 58.58 g, protein 18.64 g, dietary fibre 16.8 g. Which reading of the two labels is correct?
questions.a: Wafers have more energy and fat but less protein and fibre than chana
o: Wafers have more energy and fat but less protein and fibre than chana
Chana has more fat than wafers because it has more protein
Wafers have more carbohydrate than chana, so they are the more nutritious snack
Chana gives more energy than wafers because it has more fibre

questions.q: Two cousins live in one house: a 9-year-old and a 16-year-old sports trainee. (a) Name two factors from the chapter that make their nutrient needs differ. (b) Why can one printed diet chart not suit both?
questions.a: (a) age and physical activity (b) a balanced diet is matched to each person's needs, which vary with such factors.
s: (a) two correct factors
(b) needs differ by person, so the right amount of nutrients differs

questions.q: Ritu eats a whole 25 g packet of potato wafers whose label reads 'Energy per 100 g: 536 kcal'. She says she has eaten 536 kcal. Which correction is right?
questions.a: She ate about 134 kcal, a quarter of the per-100 g value
o: She ate about 134 kcal, a quarter of the per-100 g value
She ate 536 kcal, since a label always gives the packet value
She ate about 2,144 kcal, four times the label value
She ate about 21 kcal, since 25 g is a very small amount

questions.q:
A school's five-day lunch plan is: Monday, rice, tuar dal and a green leafy vegetable; Tuesday, noodles, a boiled egg and a carbonated drink; Wednesday, roti, paneer, salad and curd; Thursday, potato wafers and a candy bar; Friday, bajra roti, moong dal and guava. This term the principal can change the menu of only one day, and wants to replace the day that is furthest from a balanced meal.
(a) On which days does the plan serve foods that the chapter names as junk food? Name them.
(b) On how many days is there a body-building (protein-rich) food? Name one for each such day.
(c) What percentage of the five days serves a named junk food?
(d) Which day should the principal change? Give two reasons from your answers.
questions.a: (a) Tuesday (carbonated drink) and Thursday (potato wafers and a candy bar). (b) Four days: Monday (tuar dal), Tuesday (boiled egg), Wednesday (paneer), Friday (moong dal). (c) 2/5 = 40%. (d) Thursday: it has two named junk foods, and unlike every other day it has no body-building food at all, so it is furthest from a balanced meal.
s: Tuesday and Thursday, with the junk items
four days, with tuar dal, boiled egg, paneer and moong dal
Thursday: two junk foods and no protein-rich or protective food

questions.q: Explain, as a chain of three linked steps from the chapter, why eating potato wafers, candy bars and carbonated drinks frequently is not good for the body.
questions.a: These foods have high calories because of their high sugar and fat content; they contain very low amounts of proteins, minerals, vitamins and dietary fibre; so eating them often can make a person obese, and such a person may suffer from several health problems.
s: high calories from high sugar and fat
very little protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre
frequent eating can make a person obese, leading to health problems

questions.q:
(a) A balanced diet contains two components that the chapter says are not nutrients. Name them.
(b) Mira's diet has all five major nutrients but very little water and no fruit, vegetables or wholegrains. Explain why it is still not a balanced diet.
questions.a: (a) Dietary fibre (roughage) and water. (b) A balanced diet must have all essential nutrients plus roughage and water in the right amount; without water her body cannot absorb nutrients and remove waste well, and without roughage undigested food is not cleared smoothly.
s: (a) roughage and water
(b) a balanced diet needs roughage and water too, with what each does

questions.q: Show that a diet made only of potato wafers cannot be a balanced diet.
questions.a: Wafers are low in proteins, minerals, vitamins and fibre. A balanced diet needs all nutrients, roughage and water in the right amount, so wafers alone leave gaps.
s: wafers are low in protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre
a balanced diet needs all nutrients, roughage and water
so the diet has gaps and cannot be balanced

questions.q: A packet of flour travels 300 km from the farm to a mill, 200 km to a warehouse, 40 km to a shop and 3 km to Raj's home. Raj says its food miles are 3 km. Which is correct?
questions.a: 543 km, the whole distance from producer to consumer
o: 543 km, the whole distance from producer to consumer
3 km, since only the trip from the shop to home counts
40 km, the last distance that the packet went by truck
300 km, since only the distance from the farm counts

questions.q:
Statement 1: Jowar, bajra, ragi and sanwa are native crops of India that are small-sized grains.
Statement 2: Reducing food miles raises the cost and pollution of transport.
Statement 3: Once food reaches the plate, it does not matter whether any of it is wasted.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q: Show that the food miles of a packet of flour can never be less than the distance from the mill to the shop.
questions.a: Food miles are the entire distance travelled by the food from the producer to the consumer. That journey includes every leg (farm to mill, mill to shop, shop to home), and the mill-to-shop leg is only one part of it. Adding the other legs, which are zero or more, cannot make the total smaller than that one leg.
s: food miles are the whole producer-to-consumer distance
the mill-to-shop leg is one part of that journey
adding the other legs can only keep or raise the total

questions.q:
Justify the statement 'Millets deserve a place in a school's weekly menu' using the chapter.
(i) What does the chapter say about the place of millets in India's food history?
(ii) Why are millets called nutri-cereals?
(iii) Name two deficiency disorders from the chapter that a millet-rich menu could help guard against, linking each to a mineral in millets. (2 marks)
(iv) The school is in a district with uncertain rainfall and wants to buy from nearby farmers. Why do millets suit this plan?
questions.a: (i) Millets such as jowar, bajra, ragi and sanwa are native crops of India and have been an integral part of the Indian diet for centuries. (ii) They are good sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre. (iii) Anaemia, from lack of iron; bone and tooth decay, from lack of calcium. (iv) Millets can be easily cultivated in different climatic conditions, so nearby farmers can grow them, which also keeps food miles low.
s: native crops, part of the Indian diet for centuries
vitamins, iron, calcium and fibre
anaemia linked to iron
bone and tooth decay linked to calcium
easily grown in different climates, so local supply with fewer food miles

questions.q:
A packet of flour travels 120 km from the farm to the mill, 80 km from the mill to the shop and 10 km from the shop to a home.
(a) What percentage of its food miles is the farm-to-mill leg (one decimal place)?
(b) A family's choice of shop can change only the last leg. Why would buying flour from wheat grown and milled near the town cut the food miles far more?
questions.a: (a) 120/210 = 57.1%. (b) The farm-to-mill and mill-to-shop legs (200 km of the 210 km) are much longer than the 10 km shop-to-home leg, so shortening them cuts far more of the distance.
s: (b) the long early legs (200 of 210 km) are cut, not just the 10 km last leg

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Millets can be grown in different climatic conditions.
Reason (R): Millets are also called nutri-cereals.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: True or False? Because millets are small-sized grains, they give less nutrition than cereals with bigger grains. Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Millets are small-sized grains but highly nutritious: they are good sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre, which is why they are called nutri-cereals.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: small size does not mean less nutrition; millets are rich in vitamins, iron, calcium and fibre (nutri-cereals)

questions.q: A school dietitian wants a cereal that adds iron and calcium to the hostel menu. Which choice fits the chapter?
questions.a: Ragi, a millet that supplies minerals like iron and calcium
o: Ragi, a millet that supplies minerals like iron and calcium
Maize, because it is one of the millets named in the chapter
Sugarcane, because it gives instant energy to the students
Polished rice, because every cereal is a protective nutrient

questions.q:
A family in Bhopal uses 30 kg of wheat flour a month. Flour from wheat grown about 800 km away costs Rs 36 per kg at the supermarket. Flour from a neighbourhood mill, using wheat grown about 60 km away, costs Rs 40 per kg. The family has agreed to pay up to Rs 150 more a month for food with fewer food miles.
(a) Which flour has fewer food miles?
(b) Find how much more the local flour costs per month.
(c) Find the extra cost in a year.
(d) Which flour should the family buy under its own rule? Give two benefits from the chapter that it gains.
questions.a: (a) The neighbourhood mill's flour (about 60 km against 800 km). (b) 30 x 40 - 30 x 36 = Rs 120. (c) Rs 1,440. (d) The local flour, since Rs 120 a month is within the Rs 150 limit; it cuts transport cost and pollution, supports local farmers and keeps the food fresh.
s: the local flour (about 60 km against 800 km)
local flour, as Rs 120 is within Rs 150, with two benefits of fewer food miles

questions.q: Suggest one way a school canteen can cut food miles and one way it can cut food wastage, using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Buy from local producers; serve and take only as much food as can be consumed.
s: one way to cut food miles, such as using local produce
one way to cut wastage, such as taking only what can be eaten

questions.q: Which change actually reduces the food miles of a school's rice?
questions.a: Buying from a farm 20 km away instead of 900 km away
o: Buying from a farm 20 km away instead of 900 km away
Storing the same rice in the godown for a longer time
Packing the same rice in smaller bags at the same mill
Walking rather than driving to the same faraway shop

questions.q: Seema says, 'Millets alone are enough for all the nutritional needs of the body.' (a) What does the chapter say millets are good sources of? (b) Why is her statement not safe?
questions.a: (a) vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre. (b) Millets contribute to a balanced diet; a balanced diet needs all essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amount, not one food alone.
s: (a) vitamins, iron and calcium minerals, dietary fibre
(b) a balanced diet needs all components in the right amount, so millets contribute but one food is not enough

questions.q: A truck carries wheat 50 km from the farm to a mill and 30 km from the mill to a shop. Mrs Rao drives 5 km from her home to the shop without the wheat and 5 km back home with a bag of it. Counted as the chapter defines food miles, the wheat's food miles are ___ km.
A village in India has uncertain weather and the rain pattern changes from year to year. Which feature of millets makes them a sensible crop for the farmers there?
questions.a: They can be cultivated easily in varied climates
o: They can be cultivated easily in varied climates
They grow only in one fixed season of one region
They need plenty of water, so rain helps them most
They are imported grains that need special care

questions.q:
Two schools in the same district plan a lunch. School A serves rice brought from 1,500 km away and potatoes from 800 km away. School B serves jowar roti from grain grown 30 km away and vegetables from farms 10 km away. Rainfall in the district is uncertain.
(i) Which lunch has fewer food miles, and how many times farther did School A's rice travel than School B's grain?
(ii) Give two benefits of School B's lower food miles.
(iii) Which lunch includes a millet, and which feature of millets suits this district?
(iv) School A's planner says, 'Rice is nutritious too, so food miles do not matter.' Evaluate this.
(v) Give one habit from the chapter that both schools should follow at lunch to respect the work of farmers.
questions.a: (i) School B; 1500/30 = 50 times. (ii) Lower cost and pollution of transport, support for local farmers, or fresher and healthier food. (iii) School B (jowar); millets can be easily cultivated in different climatic conditions. (iv) Not right: food miles matter for transport cost, pollution, local farmers and freshness, whatever the nutrients of the food. (v) Take only as much food as can be eaten, so that none is wasted.
s: School B; 50 times
two benefits of fewer food miles
School B's jowar, easily grown in different climates
food miles matter for cost, pollution, farmers and freshness, not only nutrients
take only as much food as can be eaten

questions.q: Write a short supply situation (two or three lines) in which the food miles of a town's wheat rise, and state two consequences the chapter suggests.
questions.a: A town stops buying from a nearby farm and buys from a farm 900 km away; transport cost and pollution rise and the local farmers lose a market.
s: situation where the producer-to-consumer distance grows
transport cost and pollution rise
local farmers are less supported, or the food is less fresh

questions.q: Mohan lists the steps of the story of chapati. Which order matches the farm-to-plate diagram in the chapter?
questions.a: Growing wheat, threshing and winnowing, storage, grinding and packing, transport to the retail shop, food on the plate
o: Growing wheat, threshing and winnowing, storage, grinding and packing, transport to the retail shop, food on the plate
Growing wheat, storage, threshing and winnowing, transport to the retail shop, grinding and packing, food on the plate
Threshing and winnowing, growing wheat, grinding and packing, storage, transport to the retail shop, food on the plate
Growing wheat, grinding and packing, threshing and winnowing, storage, food on the plate, transport to the retail shop

questions.q:
Sanwa is less familiar than wheat in many homes.
(a) Give two features that, according to the chapter, sanwa shares with jowar, bajra and ragi.
(b) Which of those features explains why all four are called nutri-cereals?
questions.a: (a) Any two: they are small-sized grains; native crops of India; easily cultivated in different climatic conditions; good sources of vitamins, minerals and fibre. (b) Being good sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre.
s: (a) two shared features of millets
(b) rich in vitamins, iron and calcium, and fibre

questions.q:
A hostel throws away about 15 kg of chapatis every week.
(a) Name two stages of the farm-to-plate story of chapati whose work is wasted along with them.
(b) What does the chapter ask each person to do so that less food is wasted?
questions.a: (a) Any two: the farmer growing wheat; threshing and winnowing; storage of grains; grinding and packing; transport to the retail shop. (b) Take only as much food as one can eat, remembering the time and effort of farmers and others in bringing it to the plate.
s: (a) two stages of the farm-to-plate journey
(b) take only as much food as can be eaten

questions.q: Isha says, 'Reducing food miles keeps food fresh and cuts transport cost, but it has nothing to do with pollution.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Freshness and cost are benefits the chapter gives, but the chapter also says reducing food miles cuts pollution during transport.
s: Verdict: partly right
freshness and cost are correct
pollution is wrong: the chapter says transport pollution is cut

questions.q:
A hostel mess in Bengaluru uses 40 kg of rice a day and will replace a quarter of it with ragi. Supplier X buys ragi from farmers 60 km away and charges Rs 46 per kg. Supplier Y sells ragi brought from 900 km away at Rs 44 per kg. The mess rule is: choose the supplier with fewer food miles unless its price per kg is more than 10% higher.
(a) Name two minerals that the chapter says millets supply.
(b) How many kg of ragi will the mess buy each day?
(c) By what percentage is Supplier X's price higher than Supplier Y's (one decimal place)?
(d) Which supplier does the rule choose? Give two benefits from the chapter of that choice.
questions.a: (a) Iron and calcium. (b) 10 kg. (c) (46 - 44)/44 = 4.5%. (d) Supplier X, since 4.5% is not more than 10%; it supports local farmers and cuts transport cost and pollution, and the ragi stays fresh.
s: iron and calcium
Supplier X (4.5% is within 10%), with two benefits of fewer food miles
